passage:
Saturday
Dear Diary,
We WON again! 3-1 against Green House. I wore my red shirt, the one with the torn pocket. That makes four wins in the red shirt. The two times we lost, it was in the wash. So it is the shirt. It must be.
Urmila akka says that's silly. She says we won today because Irfan came back from his holiday and he's our best goalie. And Green House had only nine players. I told her she doesn't understand football.
Amma says I can't wear it every day because it smells. I'm going to wash it myself on Friday night so it's ready for the final.
- Darshan (Amma's lucky boy)

qa.q: What was today's score, and against which team?
qa.a: 3-1 against Green House.

qa.q: Why is Darshan so sure the red shirt makes the team win?
qa.a: He has seen four wins with the shirt on and losses when it was in the wash, so the pattern feels like proof, and he enjoys feeling lucky.

qa.q: What could help Darshan test his idea?
qa.a: He could write down each match with who played, how many players the other team had and what he wore, and see whether things like Irfan being back matter more.

qa.q: How does Urmila akka see the red shirt?
qa.a: She thinks it's silly and sees other reasons for the win: Irfan being back in goal and Green House having only nine players.

grounding: It shows a boy linking his red shirt to his team's wins just because the two keep happening together.

passage:
In Vadipatti, the under-12 kabaddi team practised on the dry field behind the temple. Muthu had noticed something. Every match he played in his faded red shirt, the team won. The week it tore and he wore blue, they lost to the next village.
"It's the shirt," he told his sister Shalini, holding it up like a flag. "It brings the luck."
Shalini, sewing the tear by lamplight, looked up. "That week, wasn't Selvam down with fever? And Kavitha teacher had gone to her mother's village, so nobody made you practise."
Muthu frowned. "That's also true."
"So which one did it, the shirt or the missing people?"
He pulled the shirt on anyway. "Maybe both. I'm not taking the chance."

qa.q: What happened the week Muthu wore blue?
qa.a: They lost to the next village.

qa.q: Why does Muthu still pull the shirt on after Shalini's questions?
qa.a: He half sees her point, but the pattern of wins still feels real, and wearing the shirt feels safer than risking a loss.

qa.q: How could Kavitha teacher help the team think about the shirt?
qa.a: She could list with them what was different on the losing day, like Selvam being ill and no practice, so they see other reasons for winning and losing.

qa.q: What would change if Muthu kept wearing the red shirt but the team stopped practising?
qa.a: They might start losing even with the shirt on, which would show that the shirt was never what made them win.

grounding: It shows a village boy deciding his red shirt causes wins because the shirt and the wins appeared together.

passage:
Tariq pulled the red T-shirt over his head and tucked it under his team vest. It was Thursday in the sports hall in Leeds, and the Hawks had won every game he'd worn it.
"You're wearing that again?" Liam asked, lacing his trainers.
"Five games, five wins. It's the shirt."
"We also got Coach Dunn five games ago," Liam said. "She's the one who makes us do passing drills every Tuesday."
Tariq tugged at the collar. That was true too. But the red shirt felt warm and lucky, like it was on his side.
They won again, 22-18. Liam scored eight of the points.
In the changing room, Tariq folded the shirt carefully. "See?"
Liam just shook his head and grinned.

qa.q: What was the score of Thursday's game?
qa.a: They won again, 22-18.

qa.q: What does Tariq's careful folding of the shirt suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he treats the shirt as special and truly believes it helps, because the lucky feeling is comforting even after Liam's point about the coach.

qa.q: What might Liam say to help Tariq see what is really changing the results?
qa.a: Liam could point out that the wins began when Coach Dunn started the Tuesday passing drills, and suggest trying one game without the shirt.

qa.q: How might Coach Dunn feel if the team gave the red shirt the credit?
qa.a: She might feel a little overlooked, since her passing drills may be doing much of the work.

grounding: It shows a boy crediting his red T-shirt for his team's winning run because the two happened together.

passage:
At the Saturday relay practice at the community sports club, Coach Nair called out the teams. Zubin, ten, came out of the changing room in his red T-shirt, the one with the faded number 7.
"You wore that last week too," Afreen said, tying her laces.
"Because we won last week. And the week before. Both times, red shirt." Zubin counted on his fingers. "The time we lost, it was in the wash. So it's the shirt."
"We also had Kartik back last week. He's the fastest."
"That's different. Kartik is just one person. The shirt is every time."
When his team won again, Zubin tugged the shirt proudly and told the coach he would wear it to the district meet. Afreen rolled her eyes and went to drink water.

qa.q: What number was on Zubin's red T-shirt?
qa.a: A faded number 7.

qa.q: How does Zubin feel about his red shirt, and what shows it?
qa.a: Zubin feels confident and proud about the shirt, tugging it after the win and planning to wear it to the district meet, because every win he remembers came with it.

qa.q: What could help Zubin check whether the shirt really matters?
qa.a: He could keep a simple list of races with and without the shirt, and also note who ran each time, to see what really changed the result.

qa.q: How does Afreen see Zubin's red-shirt idea?
qa.a: Afreen thinks Kartik coming back explains the wins better and finds the shirt idea silly, which shows in the eye-roll.

grounding: It shows a boy noticing his team wins when he wears his red shirt and deciding the shirt causes the wins.

passage:
I'm Kalyani, and I stayed with my aunt's family in Jaipur for the summer. My cousin Hrishi, nine, has a red shirt he calls "the match shirt". On every night his football club played on TV, he put it on before dinner.
The first week the club won twice, and he said, "See? Red shirt, win." On Thursday Ritu, his little sister, hid the shirt as a joke. The club lost. Hrishi was furious with her, really furious, and said she had made them lose.
I don't know if he truly believed it or just needed someone to blame. But by Sunday he was checking the shirt was clean on Saturday night.
Ritu whispered to me that the club's best player had been injured on Thursday. She said it very quietly, like she didn't want Hrishi to hear.

qa.q: What did Ritu do on Thursday?
qa.a: She hid the shirt as a joke.

qa.q: Why might Hrishi be so sure the shirt made the club lose?
qa.a: The shirt and the wins kept showing up together, so when the shirt was missing and the club lost, it felt like proof to Hrishi that one caused the other.

qa.q: How could Kalyani help Hrishi see what else happened on Thursday?
qa.a: Kalyani could calmly bring up the injured best player and ask Hrishi which seems more likely to change a match, a shirt at home or a missing player.

qa.q: What is it like for Ritu to be blamed for the loss?
qa.a: Ritu probably feels hurt and a bit scared of Hrishi's anger, which is why she whispers about the injured player instead of saying it out loud 😔

grounding: It shows a boy linking his red shirt to his team's wins and deciding the shirt causes them, because the two happen together.
